findings.title: The JSON Schema validator is marshalled and recompiled from scratch on every request
findings.impact: Every request against a 3.1 document pays a full schema marshal and JSON Schema compile, work that is proportional to the size of the declared schema rather than to the size of the client's payload. That is an asymmetric cost an unauthenticated client can drive with minimal effort: small requests, large server-side work, and the amplification grows with the size of the API's schemas.
findings.evidence: useJSONSchema2020 (line 204) calls newJSONSchemaValidator(schema) on every invocation, and newJSONSchemaValidator does four things per call: json.Marshal of the whole schema tree (line 21), json.Unmarshal into map[string]any (line 27), a recursive rewrite of that map (transformOpenAPIToJSONSchema, line 57), and a fresh jsonschema.NewCompiler + AddResource + Compile (lines 35-48). Nothing caches the result: the compiler and the compiled schema are stored on a jsonSchemaValidator value that is discarded when validate returns, and there is no package-level map keyed by schema, unlike the compiledPatterns cache the same package keeps for regexes (openapi3/schema.go:46). openapi3filter reaches this once per parameter and once per body for every OpenAPI 3.1 request (validate_request.go:243 and :355) and once per response (validate_response.go:77).

findings.title: A failed pattern compile leaves a nil RegexMatcher that is then dereferenced, panicking the validator
findings.impact: Any request whose value reaches that string schema panics the validating goroutine. Under net/http the panic is recovered per connection, so the practical effect is a dropped connection and a stack trace in the logs for every affected request; when the same validation runs outside an HTTP handler - a worker, a CLI, a batch job - the process dies.
findings.evidence: openapi3/schema.go:2654-2678. `cp, _ := cpiface.(RegexMatcher)` leaves cp nil on a cache miss; `if cp == nil { if cp, err = schema.compilePattern(settings.regexCompiler); err != nil { if !settings.multiError { return err }; me = append(me, err) } }`. In the multiError branch execution falls out of that if and reaches `if !cp.MatchString(value)` at line 2666 with a cp that compilePattern never produced. Both compiler branches of compilePattern (openapi3/schema_pattern.go:16-33) leave it unusable: a custom RegexCompilerFunc that returns (nil, err) leaves a nil interface, and the default branch `cp, err = regexp.Compile(intoGoRegexp(pattern))` leaves an interface holding a nil *regexp.Regexp, whose MatchString dereferences the nil receiver. Either way line 2666 panics. The error path records the error and then uses the value the error said could not be produced.

findings.title: An array index taken from the query string sizes an allocation in deepObject parameter decoding
findings.impact: An unauthenticated client turns a ~30-byte query string into ~2e9 loop iterations and tens of gigabytes of []any backing store inside the request goroutine, before a single schema keyword is evaluated. The process is killed by the OOM killer or wedged; availability loss is process-wide, so it reaches every other user of the service and not only the sender.
findings.evidence: sliceMapToSlice converts a map keyed by decimal array indexes into a slice, and the keys arrive from the query string unmodified. urlValuesDecoder.DecodeObject (line 663, case "deepObject") matches every query key against `^<param>\[` and stores the bracket contents as map keys; makeObject (line 911) deepSets them into a nested map; buildResObj (line 965, case schema type "array") calls sliceMapToSlice on that map. Inside sliceMapToSlice the only processing of a key is strconv.Atoi (line 942); `max` is then the largest key seen (lines 949-954) and the loop is `for i := 0; i <= max; i++ { result = append(result, ...) }` (lines 955-963). No line compares `max` with a configured maximum, with len(m), or with anything else the client does not choose. buildResObj then does `resultArr := make([]any /*not 0,*/, len(arr))` at line 986 on the returned slice. findings.title: Neither workflow declares a permissions block, so the repository token runs at the inherited default
findings.impact: If the inherited default is read+write, every step in the job - including third-party code resolved from a movable reference - holds a token that can push commits, move tags, edit issues and create releases on this repository. If the default is read-only the exposure is a read of repository content, which is public anyway.
findings.evidence: Neither .github/workflows/go.yml nor .github/workflows/shellcheck.yml contains a `permissions:` key at workflow or job level, so both inherit the repository or organization default for GITHUB_TOKEN. go.yml compounds it by exporting the token to every step of build-and-test through the job-level env block (`GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}`), rather than attaching it to the one step that needs it; the steps that receive it include the unpinned third-party actions and the three `@latest` tools of F-006. Least privilege applies per job, and no job here declares any.

findings.title: CI executes third-party code from mutable references, including three tools resolved at @latest
findings.impact: Whoever controls any of those upstream tags or module versions - or anyone who compromises the account that can move them - executes arbitrary code on the runner with the repository token in scope, on every push and pull request. This is the exact shape of the tj-actions/changed-files incident (CVE-2025-30066), where every tag from v1 to v45.0.7 was repointed at a commit that dumped runner secrets into the log.
findings.evidence: Zero of the seven `uses:` references under .github/workflows are pinned by a 40-character commit SHA. go.yml: actions/setup-go@v6 (twice), actions/cache@v3, actions/checkout@v6 (twice). shellcheck.yml: actions/checkout@v2 and ludeeus/action-shellcheck@1.1.0. A git tag is a movable pointer, so each of those names resolves to whatever commit the tag points at when the job runs. Three steps go further and resolve third-party Go programs at run time with no version at all: `go run golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis/passes/modernize/cmd/modernize@latest -test -diff -fix ...` and `go run golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis/passes/nilness/cmd/nilness@latest ./...` in go.yml, and `go install github.com/incu6us/goimports-reviser/v3@latest` in the check-goimports job. findings.title: ZipFileBodyDecoder decodes without an expansion bound and appends whole buffers regardless of bytes read
findings.impact: None by default: init() (line 1334) does not register this decoder for any media type, so it runs only if the consumer calls RegisterBodyDecoder("application/zip", ZipFileBodyDecoder) themselves, having read the warning attached to it. A consumer that does opt in inherits an unbounded decompression path, and the decoded string it validates against its schema is not the archive's contents.
findings.evidence: The whole body is buffered (io.Copy into a bytes.Buffer, line 1615) and then every entry of the archive is read into `content` with no ceiling on the total: `content := make([]byte, 0, bufferSize*len(zr.File))` followed by an unbounded append loop across all entries (lines 1622-1651). Its own doc comment says so: "Use with caution as this implementation may be susceptible to a zip bomb attack." Separately, the read loop is `n, err := rc.Read(buffer); if 0 < n { content = append(content, buffer...) }` (lines 1636-1639) - it appends the full 256-byte buffer rather than `buffer[:n]`, so every short read pads the decoded value with stale bytes from the previous read.

findings.title: The legacy router collapses paths that differ only by a trailing slash, and picks the winner from Go map order
findings.impact: Two effects. When a document declares both forms, which operation a request is validated against is decided at process start by map iteration order, so two replicas of the same service can enforce different parameters, different body schemas and different `security` requirements for the same URL; if one of the two operations declares `security: []` or a weaker scheme, that is an authorization check that applies or not depending on the roll of a map. When only one form is declared, the router accepts both, so a request the downstream mux routes to handler B may have been validated against operation A - net/http's ServeMux and most Go frameworks treat `/foo` and `/foo/` as different routes, while this router does not.
findings.evidence: Both halves of the trie strip trailing slashes unconditionally: CreateNode does `for strings.HasSuffix(path, "/") { path = path[:len(path)-1] }` at lines 168-170, and Match does the identical loop at lines 257-259. So the spec paths `/foo` and `/foo/` create the same node, and whichever operation is added second overwrites the first's Value (node.Value = value, node.go:160). routers/legacy.NewRouter adds them in `for path, pathItem := range doc.Paths.Map()` (routers/legacy/router.go:67) - a Go map range, whose order is randomised per process. Document validation does not catch the collision: Paths.Validate compares normalizeTemplatedPath outputs (openapi3/paths.go:64-75), and normalizeTemplatedPath returns the path untouched when it contains no '{' (paths.go:229-231) and never touches a trailing slash, so `/foo` and `/foo/` are not reported as conflicting paths. findings.title: External $ref resolution has one all-or-nothing switch, and the default reader has no timeout and no egress allowlist
findings.impact: A consumer that turns the flag on to resolve its own multi-file specification, and later loads a document it did not author, makes the process fetch whatever URL the document names: loopback services, internal hosts, and the cloud metadata endpoint, from the process's own network position, plus arbitrary local files through the file branch. Because there is no timeout, a reference to a host that accepts and never answers pins the goroutine and the loaded-document slot indefinitely, which is a cheaper attack than the fetch itself. Redirects are followed with the default policy, so an allowlist a consumer builds by inspecting the URL before calling the loader does not survive a 302.
findings.evidence: DefaultReadFromURI is `URIMapCache(ReadFromURIs(ReadFromHTTP(http.DefaultClient), ReadFromFile))` (line 46). http.DefaultClient has no Timeout and the default redirect policy, and ReadFromHTTP passes the location straight to cl.Do with no scheme, host or address check (lines 51-70); its own comment says the client "may be customized to implement timeouts", i.e. the shipped one is not. ReadFromFile likewise reads any path the URL carries after path.Clean (lines 79-84), with no base-directory containment. The only control the library offers over this is the boolean Loader.IsExternalRefsAllowed (openapi3/loader.go:32), enforced at openapi3/loader.go:118 and :349; once it is true, every `$ref` in the document is fetched. The consequence is documented in the tree, but on the neighbouring field: the SECURITY note on ReadFromURIFunc (loader.go:41-48) spells out `$ref: "/etc/passwd"` and `$ref:

findings.title: The process-global compiled-pattern cache is never evicted and ignores which regex engine produced an entry
findings.impact: In a long-lived process that loads or validates documents it did not author - a spec linter, a gateway that reloads specs, a SaaS that accepts uploaded OpenAPI files - memory grows without bound in proportion to the number of distinct patterns seen, and it is never reclaimed. Separately, a consumer that installed a stricter or differently-flavoured regex engine may silently get the Go engine's verdict for a pattern another document already cached, so the matcher that decides whether input is acceptable is not the one the consumer configured.
findings.evidence: compiledPatterns is a package-level sync.Map (openapi3/schema.go:46). compilePattern stores into it with `compiledPatterns.Store(pattern, cp)` (schema_pattern.go:34) and visitJSONString reads it with `compiledPatterns.Load(schema.Pattern)` (schema.go:2655). Those three lines are every reference to it in non-test code; there is no Delete, no size limit and no TTL. Two consequences follow from the key being the raw pattern string alone. First, every distinct `pattern` string any document has ever declared stays resident for the life of the process. Second, compilePattern takes the compiler as an argument (`c RegexCompilerFunc`) but the key does not record it, so an entry compiled by the default Go engine during doc.Validate is later handed to a caller that asked for a custom engine through openapi3filter.Options.RegexCompiler or openapi3.SetSchemaRegexCompiler, and vice versa across docume

findings.title: OpenAPI 3.1 request validation silently falls back to a validator that ignores every 2020-12 keyword
findings.impact: Request bodies and parameters that violate a declared 3.1 constraint are accepted as valid. The sharpest case is a tuple schema (`prefixItems` with no `items`), where the fallback validates no array element at all, and `unevaluatedProperties: false` / `propertyNames` / `dependentRequired`, where the fallback lets through properties and combinations the specification forbids. Because the fallback is silent, the operator sees a validator that reports success.
findings.evidence: openapi3filter turns on the JSON Schema 2020-12 validator automatically for every OpenAPI 3.1 document, at three sites: validate_request.go:243 (parameters), validate_request.go:355 (request body) and validate_response.go:77 (responses), each `if ... IsOpenAPI31OrLater() { opts = append(opts, openapi3.EnableJSONSchema2020()) }`. Schema.VisitJSON then routes to useJSONSchema2020 (openapi3/schema.go:1945). useJSONSchema2020 reads: `validator, err := newJSONSchemaValidator(schema); if err != nil { return schema.visitJSON(settings, value) }` - on ANY construction error it returns the built-in validator's verdict, with no error, no log and no flag on the result. newJSONSchemaValidator fails when compiler.Compile returns an error (lines 45-48). The compiled resource is the schema marshalled standalone, and SchemaRef.MarshalYAML (openapi3/refs.go:1049-1053) emits `{"$ref": "..."}` for every ref

advisories_to_match.summary: kin-openapi has uncontrolled resource consumption in openapi3filter deepObject query parameter decoding
advisories_to_match.description:
### Summary

An uncontrolled resource consumption vulnerability in `openapi3filter` lets any unauthenticated client force multi-gigabyte heap allocation with a single, tiny HTTP request. When a spec declares a `deepObject`-style query parameter whose schema contains an array (a normal, documented pattern), the decoder reconstructs the array by reading the **largest attacker-supplied index** and allocating one slot for every position from `0` up to that index — *before* schema validation (including `maxItems`) ever runs. A request as small as 24 bytes (`?param[items][50000000]=x`) drives heap allocation to **~6.1 GiB**, reliably triggering an OOM kill / restart loop on memory-constrained services.

### Details

The OpenAPI `style: deepObject` serialization lets clients express arrays in the query string using bracket notation, e.g. `param[items][0]=a&param[items][1]=b`. The decoder first collects these into an intermediate `map[string]any` keyed by the string of the index, then converts that sparse map into a real `[]any` in [`sliceMapToSlice`](https://github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/blob/master/openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go#L936):
